screens.title: Performance Tuning and Optimization for Fabric Networks
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore the practical levers you control to tune a Hyperledger Fabric network. You will learn how orderer batching, peer resources, database selection, chaincode efficiency, and endorsement policies interact to affect throughput and latency. We will use concrete examples you can replicate in the test-network: changing BatchTimeout to see block cutting frequency, choosing CouchDB and adding indexes for rich queries, and profiling chaincode to find hotspots. You’ll also learn common mistakes to avoid, like forgetting CouchDB indexes or using overly broad endorsement policies. This chapter is hands-on and measurement-focused: you’ll not only change configuration values but also monitor transaction throughput, latency, block finalization, and resource utilization. By the end you should be able to decide when to increase batch sizes, when to reduce timeouts, which state database suits your query patterns, and how to design chaincode and keys to avoid MVCC conflicts. Think of this as a system-level tuning checklist that balances trade-offs: faster blocks versus higher propagation cost, simpler queries versus richer JSON-based queries, and security vs. endorsement cost. Ready to explore the knobs that control Fabric performance?

Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Performance Tuning
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Performance Tuning and Optimization for Fabric Networks

Understand the knobs that control transaction throughput and latency, and learn measurement-led strategies to tune peers, orderers, databases, and chaincode.

In this lesson

You will change BatchTimeout to observe block frequency, compare LevelDB and CouchDB trade-offs, add CouchDB indexes, and profile chaincode to reduce endorsement latency.

Why it matters

Proper tuning prevents bottlenecks and avoids wasted resources while meeting application SLAs for latency and throughput.

Quick key idea

Tune batching and resources to match the expected transaction pattern. Use CouchDB when you need rich queries and add indexes; use LevelDB when simple lookups dominate.

overview

Orderer
BatchSize, BatchTimeout, block finalization
State DB
LevelDB vs CouchDB trade-offs
Explore key topics
Batching parameters

Database choice
When to prefer CouchDB for rich queries and when LevelDB is sufficient.
Chaincode & MVCC
Reduce hot-key contention and profile chaincode to speed endorsements.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives focus your work: identify the main factors affecting Fabric performance, tune peers and orderers, choose and configure peer state databases, optimize chaincode and endorsement policies, and measure performance using standard metrics. First, you will learn to identify throughput and latency drivers across endorsement, ordering, validation, and commit stages, and recognize how network latency and infrastructure constrain them. Second, you will gain hands-on skill in adjusting orderer BatchSize and BatchTimeout to match transaction patterns, balancing block frequency against propagation cost. Third, you will learn how LevelDB differs from CouchDB and why CouchDB requires indexes for efficient rich queries. Finally, you will practice profiling chaincode to remove hotspots and design endorsement policies that meet security needs without unnecessary latency. Each objective includes a small, practical milestone so you can verify competency: for example, change BatchTimeout and observe block creation intervals, or add a CouchDB index and see query latency drop. These objectives are chosen to ensure you can both reason about trade-offs and make measured configuration choices in a real network. Keep these goals in mind as you work through the hands-on steps and monitoring examples in the following screens.

screens.title: What drives Fabric performance?
screens.narratorSegment: Performance in Fabric is a system property. It emerges from how transactions are processed: endorsement (peers execute and produce read/write sets), ordering (the orderer groups transactions into blocks), validation (peers check endorsement and MVCC), and commit (state updates). Each stage contributes latency and can limit throughput. For example, slow chaincode execution lengthens endorsement time; a conservative BatchTimeout delays block creation; overloaded peers increase validation and commit delays. Network latency between components adds propagation time. Infrastructure bottlenecks such as C P U, insufficient memory, or low input and output throughput on peer hosts will show up as spikes in endorsement or commit times. A useful mental model is to trace a single transaction: client submits request, endorsing peers run chaincode and return a response, orderers batch transactions, peers validate and commit blocks. The slowest element on that path often dictates perceived latency. An actionable first step is to measure per-stage timings: how long endorsement takes, how frequently blocks are cut, and how long validation/commit takes. That data lets you focus tuning effort where it matters: faster chaincode, tuned batching, or added compute. As you proceed, remember a common misconception: improving one stage without measuring others can shift the bottleneck rather than remove it. Ask yourself after each change: what metric moved and what moved next?

keyIdea.text: End-to-end performance depends on the slowest stage in the transaction path—measure each stage before tuning.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Performance Drivers
Definition: Transaction path

Fabric processes transactions in stages: endorsement, ordering, validation (MVCC), and commit. Each contributes to latency and can limit throughput depending on workload and resources.

Key observations
  • Slow chaincode increases endorsement time and reduces effective throughput.
  • BatchTimeout controls maximum wait before a block is cut when transaction arrival is low.
  • Overloaded peers cause validation and commit delays even if ordering is fast.
Concrete example

If endorsements average 200ms and ordering plus commit adds 300ms, the total latency will be around 500ms. Reducing BatchTimeout alone may not help if endorsement is the slowest step.

Actionable checklist
  1. Measure per-stage timings: endorsement, ordering, validation, commit.
  2. Identify the slowest stage and resource constraints (CPU, memory, I/O).
  3. Apply targeted tuning or scaling, then re-measure to confirm improvement.
Common mistake

Tuning one parameter without measuring can move the bottleneck. Always measure before and after changes.

screens.title: Orderer batching: BatchSize and BatchTimeout
screens.narratorSegment: Two parameters in the ordering service shape block creation: BatchSize and BatchTimeout. BatchSize sets the maximum number of transactions or block byte size before the orderer cuts a block. BatchTimeout is the maximum time the orderer will wait before cutting a block even if BatchSize isn’t reached. Larger BatchSize usually increases throughput because more transactions are grouped, reducing per-transaction overhead and improving network and storage efficiency. However, larger blocks increase propagation time and mean an individual transaction may wait longer before being committed, increasing latency. Smaller BatchTimeout reduces latency by cutting blocks more frequently, but when transaction arrival rate is low it can lead to many small blocks and lower throughput. Choosing values depends on your workload: a sustained high transaction rate favors larger BatchSize; low but latency-sensitive traffic favors small BatchTimeout. A practical approach is to iterate: measure current TPS and latency, try doubling BatchSize or halving BatchTimeout in a dev channel, and observe orderer logs and block finalization times. Remember to recreate or update channel configuration when you change channel-scoped parameters. A common misconception is that larger BatchSize is always better — it is better only when the network can process larger blocks without propagation or validation becoming new bottlenecks.

keyIdea.title: Batching trade-off
keyIdea.text: BatchSize increases throughput but can increase latency; BatchTimeout reduces latency but may lower throughput under low load.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Orderer Batching
BatchSize and BatchTimeout explained

BatchSize: maximum number of transactions or maximum block bytes. BatchTimeout: maximum wait time before cutting a block.

Trade-offs
  • Large BatchSize: higher throughput, higher block propagation cost, increased per-transaction latency.
  • Small BatchTimeout: lower individual transaction latency, possibly lower throughput under low load.
Concrete scenario

If your app has a steady 200 TPS, a larger BatchSize can improve efficiency. If clients need sub-second confirmation at 1-2 TPS, reduce BatchTimeout to avoid waiting for enough transactions.

Practical tuning steps
  1. Establish baseline: measure TPS and latency under current settings.
  2. Adjust one parameter at a time, e.g., increase BatchSize, then measure.
  3. Recreate channel or apply config update for channel-scoped changes, and re-measure.
Pitfall

Don’t assume larger BatchSize always improves performance. If peers or network bandwidth cannot handle larger blocks, latency or propagation errors will grow.

screens.title: Hands-on: Change BatchTimeout and observe orderer logs
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows the minimal steps to change BatchTimeout in a development environment and observe the effect. Start by bringing up the test-network with defaults, then watch the orderer logs to see how often blocks are written. Next, edit configtx. yaml to change BatchTimeout from the default (often two seconds) to a new value such as five seconds or 500 milliseconds depending on your goal. Recreate the channel in the dev network so the new channel configuration takes effect. Finally, monitor the orderer logs for writeBlock messages to confirm block creation frequency changed as expected. This process is safe in a dev environment and is the quickest way to confirm tuning behavior before attempting a channel update in production. A common misconception is that changing the local orderer container setting will affect an existing channel immediately — channel-scoped batch parameters require channel config updates or channel recreation. Remember to capture metrics both before and after the change so you can quantify the impact on latency and throughput, and to test with realistic invoke scripts so BatchSize behaviors become visible when transaction rate varies.

keyIdea.text: Change BatchTimeout in configtx.yaml, recreate channel in test-network, and verify writeBlock frequency in orderer logs before applying in production.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › BatchTimeout Walkthrough
Terminal steps (dev)
cd fabric-samples/test-network
./network.sh down
./network.sh up createChannel -ca

# Edit: configtx/configtx.yaml -> change BatchTimeout: 5s

./network.sh down
./network.sh up createChannel -ca
Recreating the channel applies the profile with the new BatchTimeout. For a production channel, use a config update instead of recreation.
Verify in logs
docker logs orderer.example.com
# Look for messages like: about to write block
Example observation

If BatchTimeout goes from 2s to 5s, writeBlock entries should appear roughly every five seconds when traffic is low. If you generate many transactions quickly, blocks may be cut sooner when BatchSize limit is reached.

Check your assumptions

Always compare logs and metrics. Changing BatchTimeout without a baseline makes it hard to judge improvement. Use a short test script to generate controlled load when verifying BatchSize behavior.

screens.title: Peer resources and monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: Peers are responsible for endorsement, validation, and commitment. They run chaincode, maintain state databases, and write blocks to disk. Because of these roles, peer hosts need balanced C P U, memory, and disk input and output. Endorsement is C P U and memory heavy when chaincode executes complex logic; state writes and CouchDB queries can be input and output bound. A common operational error is under-provisioning disk input and output for peers running CouchDB, causing slow queries and backpressure. Monitoring is essential: track C P U and memory usage on peer hosts, disk input and output wait times, and network throughput. Instrument peer process metrics for endorsement durations, commit durations, and chaincode execution time. When you see endorsement time climb, profile chaincode to find inefficient loops or excessive ledger reads. When commit or validation slows, check disk input and output and peer process queue lengths. Scale horizontally by adding peers to share endorsement load or vertically by increasing C P U/memory where appropriate. Another common misconception is to scale only orderers when throughput suffers — often peers are the bottleneck. Always pair monitoring with targeted remediation: if CouchDB queries are slow, add indexes; if endorsement time is high, optimize chaincode or add endorsing peers.

keyIdea.text: Provision peers with balanced CPU, memory, and disk I/O; monitor endorsement and commit timings to detect bottlenecks early.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Peer Resources & Monitoring
What peers do

Peers endorse transactions by executing chaincode, validate transactions using MVCC, and commit blocks to the ledger. They also host the state database (LevelDB or CouchDB).

Monitor these signals
  • Endorsement duration per chaincode invocation.
  • Commit/validation duration and peer queue lengths.
  • CPU, memory, disk I/O wait, and network throughput on peer hosts.
Example action

If endorsement time is high, profile chaincode and reduce external I/O or expensive loops. If disk I/O is the limit, consider faster storage or move heavy queries to analytics off-ledger.

Scaling strategies
  1. Scale peers horizontally to distribute endorsement load.
  2. Increase CPU/memory for heavy chaincode execution.
  3. Improve disk performance for CouchDB or commit-heavy workloads.
Misconception

Scaling only orderers when throughput degrades is a mistake if peers are CPU or I/O limited. Measure before scaling.

screens.title: LevelDB vs CouchDB
screens.narratorSegment: Fabric peers support two state database options: LevelDB and CouchDB. LevelDB is the default embedded key-value store and is efficient for simple key lookups and range queries. It runs in-process and avoids network overhead, so simple read/write patterns usually perform faster with LevelDB. CouchDB is an external JSON document database that supports rich queries and indexing on non-key attributes, which is essential for applications requiring flexible filtering or queries by fields other than the ledger key. CouchDB runs as a separate process, often in another container, and introduces network and serialization overhead. For query-heavy applications that need JSON document access and indexed searches, CouchDB is generally the correct choice — provided that you create appropriate indexes. Without indexes, CouchDB will perform full database scans for rich queries, causing severe performance degradation. A practical rule: prefer LevelDB when your workload is dominated by direct key lookups or range scans; prefer CouchDB when you need expressive JSON queries and can maintain appropriate indexes. Measure query latency under realistic load in both modes before committing to one in production. Remember that choosing CouchDB also means managing an additional process and ensuring indexes are deployed with your chaincode or database configuration.

keyIdea.text: Use LevelDB for simple key-based workloads; use CouchDB for rich JSON queries but always define indexes to avoid full scans.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › LevelDB vs CouchDB
Side-by-side
LevelDB

Embedded key-value store, fast for key lookups and range queries, minimal overhead.

CouchDB

External JSON document DB, supports rich queries and indexes, adds network and process overhead.

Concrete guidance

If your application needs filters on non-key fields, use CouchDB with indexes. If you only do direct key access, prefer LevelDB for lower latency.

Indexing note

CouchDB requires JSON indexes for efficient rich queries. Without them, queries cause full scans and very poor performance. Plan index deployment with your chaincode.

Mistake to avoid

Choosing CouchDB because of flexible queries but forgetting to create indexes will make queries slow and strain the peer.

screens.title: CouchDB indexing: create an index for rich queries
screens.narratorSegment: CouchDB needs JSON index definitions so rich queries can run efficiently. An index declares the fields CouchDB should use to locate documents quickly. For example, if your application frequently queries by owner and status, you should create an index that includes those fields plus docType if you use it. Creating and deploying an index prevents full database scans. The example index is a small JSON document that names the index and lists fields. Deploy the index alongside chaincode or place it in the CouchDB design documents so the peer will use it for queries. Without this step, queries that filter by non-key attributes will degrade to full scans as the ledger grows. After deploying an index, re-run queries and measure latency — you should see a significant reduction. A common misconception is that CouchDB automatically indexes all fields; it does not. You must explicitly define indexes for the queries you plan to run frequently. Keep index definitions targeted to avoid unnecessary indexing overhead. This walkthrough provides a sample index and explains where to place it in your chaincode packaging or CouchDB configuration so it is available to peer query execution.

keyIdea.title: Index early
keyIdea.text: Define and deploy CouchDB JSON indexes for fields used by frequent rich queries to avoid full scans and poor performance.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › CouchDB Indexing
Sample index definition
{
  "index": {
    "fields": ["docType", "owner", "status"]
  },
  "name": "ownerStatusIndex",
  "ddoc": "indexOwnerStatusDoc",
  "type": "json"
}
Place this JSON in your chaincode package or deploy it to CouchDB design docs so queries that filter by owner and status use the index.
Post-deploy check

After adding the index, run the rich query and compare latency and resource usage to the pre-index baseline. Expect much lower query times for indexed fields.

Deployment tips
  • Include index files with your chaincode or deploy them via CouchDB API.
  • Target indexes to fields you query frequently to limit overhead.
  • Measure query performance before and after indexing.
Common mistake

Assuming CouchDB auto-indexes fields causes painful full scans. Explicitly define indexes for production queries.

screens.title: Chaincode efficiency and endorsement policy complexity
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode execution speed and endorsement policy complexity directly influence endorsement latency and overall transaction time. Inefficient chaincode, such as functions with unbounded loops, excessive ledger reads and writes, or repeated JSON parsing, increases endorsement duration. Profile your chaincode to find slow paths and remove unnecessary ledger operations. Use local caching where safe and avoid heavy external input and output within endorsements. Endorsement policies determine which peers must simulate transactions: broader policies require more peers to execute chaincode and respond, increasing latency. For example, an OR policy that allows any single organization to endorse is generally faster than an AND policy requiring multiple organizations. Balance security needs against performance: use narrowly targeted policies where possible and consider separating reads and writes with different endorsement requirements when the architecture allows it. MVCC conflicts happen when many transactions try to update the same key concurrently; Fabric invalidates conflicting transactions at validation. To reduce hot-key contention, shard data across multiple keys, use composite keys with unique identifiers, or design tenant-aware keys. A common misconception is that simply adding more endorsing peers always improves performance; more peers increase endorsement parallelism only if they reduce per-peer load and do not add network overhead. keyIdea.text: Optimize chaincode to shorten endorsement time and choose endorsement policies that meet trust requirements without unnecessary peers.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Chaincode & Endorsement
Make chaincode fast
  • Profile and remove expensive loops and redundant ledger reads.
  • Avoid heavy external I/O during endorsement; keep simulation local.
  • Use efficient data structures and limit JSON parsing when possible.
Example

Replacing multiple ledger reads with a single range scan or a batched query inside endorsement can reduce endorsement time significantly.

Endorsement policy choices

Prefer minimal necessary endorsements. OR policies are faster than AND policies that require many organizations to endorse every transaction. Tailor policies to the operation's trust needs.

MVCC conflict mitigation

Design keys to avoid hot spots: shard counters, use composite keys with unique suffixes, and avoid frequent updates to a single global key. This reduces invalidated transactions due to MVCC conflicts.

screens.title: Measuring and analyzing performance
screens.narratorSegment: Effective tuning depends on measurement. Collect transaction throughput (TPS), end-to-end transaction latency, block finalization time, and peer and orderer resource utilization (C P U, memory, disk input and output). Instrument chaincode to record execution times and use peer/exported metrics to capture endorsement durations and commit timings. Tools like Prometheus and Grafana provide a standard way to store and visualize these metrics so you can compare baselines and the effect of changes. When you change BatchSize or BatchTimeout, observe TPS and latency graphs over the same test script so variations are visible. Monitor block height growth and block finalization to confirm blocks are created and propagated at the expected frequency. For CouchDB-backed peers, monitor query latency and input and output wait to detect slow queries or missing indexes. A common mistake is relying on a single metric: a higher TPS number alone may hide increasing tail latency or C P U saturation. Always look at a small set of complementary metrics: TPS, median and 95th-percentile latency, block finalization, and resource utilization. Use the data to iterate: change one variable, measure, and revert if the change has negative side effects. This measurement discipline prevents blind tuning and ensures network stability.

content.html:
Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Measuring Performance
Core metrics
  • Transaction throughput (TPS)
  • Transaction latency (median, 95th percentile)
  • Block finalization time and block height growth
  • Peer and orderer CPU, memory, disk I/O
Tooling note

Prometheus and Grafana let you store and visualize these metrics so changes are visible across test runs and baselines.

Analysis workflow
  1. Create a baseline under a representative load.
  2. Change one parameter or component and re-run the test.
  3. Compare TPS, latency percentiles, and resource metrics to decide if the change improved the system.
Common pitfall

Relying solely on average latency or TPS can hide tail latency and resource spikes. Check percentiles and resource graphs together.

screens.title: Pitfalls and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: There are recurring mistakes teams make when tuning Fabric. First, forgetting CouchDB indexes for rich queries is common and costly — queries degrade to full scans and can overwhelm the peer. Second, endorsement policies that require many organizations for every transaction introduce extra endorsement latency; ensure the policy matches the operation’s trust needs. Third, failing to monitor peer C P U, memory, and disk input and output often lets resource bottlenecks remain hidden until a burst of traffic exposes them. Fourth, changing BatchSize or BatchTimeout without a measured baseline can mask negative side effects; always test changes in a staging or dev channel and collect metrics. Best practices include: define targeted CouchDB indexes and deploy them with chaincode; profile chaincode and remove hot paths; tune one variable at a time and capture before/after metrics; design keys and data structures to reduce MVCC conflicts by sharding or using composite keys; and automate metrics collection so regressions are caught early. These practices help you make incremental, reversible changes and maintain predictable performance under load. A healthy tuning process is measurement-driven, conservative in production, and experimental in staging.

Module 10 › Chapter 10.4 › Pitfalls & Best Practices
Top mistakes
  • Not creating CouchDB indexes for rich queries.
  • Overly broad endorsement policies for routine operations.
  • Ignoring peer resource monitoring and I/O constraints.
  • Tuning without a baseline and rollback plan.
Best practices
  • Measure per-stage metrics and establish baselines.
  • Change one parameter at a time and re-measure.
  • Deploy indexes with chaincode and profile chaincode regularly.
  • Design keys to avoid MVCC hot spots and shard where needed.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore the practical levers you control to tune a Hyperledger Fabric network. You will learn how orderer batching, peer resources, database selection, chaincode efficiency, and endorsement policies interact to affect throughput and latency. We will use concrete examples you can replicate in the test-network: changing BatchTimeout to see block cutting frequency, choosing CouchDB and adding indexes for rich queries, and profiling chaincode to find hotspots. You’ll also learn common mistakes to avoid, like forgetting CouchDB indexes or using overly broad endorsement policies. This chapter is hands-on and measurement-focused: you’ll not only change configuration values but also monitor transaction throughput, latency, block finalization, and resource utilization. By the end you should be able to decide when to increase batch sizes, when to reduce timeouts, which state database suits your query patterns, and how to design chaincode and keys to avoid MVCC conflicts. Think of this as a system-level tuning checklist that balances trade-offs: faster blocks versus higher propagation cost, simpler queries versus richer JSON-based queries, and security vs. endorsement cost. Ready to explore the knobs that control Fabric performance?

These learning objectives focus your work: identify the main factors affecting Fabric performance, tune peers and orderers, choose and configure peer state databases, optimize chaincode and endorsement policies, and measure performance using standard metrics. First, you will learn to identify throughput and latency drivers across endorsement, ordering, validation, and commit stages, and recognize how network latency and infrastructure constrain them. Second, you will gain hands-on skill in adjusting orderer BatchSize and BatchTimeout to match transaction patterns, balancing block frequency against propagation cost. Third, you will learn how LevelDB differs from CouchDB and why CouchDB requires indexes for efficient rich queries. Finally, you will practice profiling chaincode to remove hotspots and design endorsement policies that meet security needs without unnecessary latency. Each objective includes a small, practical milestone so you can verify competency: for example, change BatchTimeout and observe block creation intervals, or add a CouchDB index and see query latency drop. These objectives are chosen to ensure you can both reason about trade-offs and make measured configuration choices in a real network. Keep these goals in mind as you work through the hands-on steps and monitoring examples in the following screens.

This second objectives page focuses on verifiable, hands-on milestones tied to the chapter's content. First, you will change a channel's BatchTimeout and recreate the channel in a development environment, then use orderer logs to confirm that blocks are cut at the new interval. Second, you will deploy a simple chaincode and run rapid invokes to observe how BatchSize affects block creation when the transaction load spikes. Third, you will create CouchDB JSON indexes for fields your application queries frequently, and measure query latency before and after indexing. Fourth, you will capture core metrics like TPS, end-to-end transaction latency, block finalization time, and peer resource utilization so you can compare the impact of a configuration change. Each card in this set maps to a micro-task you can complete in the test-network. These tasks are intentionally practical: they require you to modify configuration, redeploy or recreate channels, and use logs and metrics to prove the effect. By completing them you will not only learn the theory of performance trade-offs but also how to operationalize tuning safely in a development or staging environment.

Performance in Fabric is a system property. It emerges from how transactions are processed: endorsement (peers execute and produce read/write sets), ordering (the orderer groups transactions into blocks), validation (peers check endorsement and MVCC), and commit (state updates). Each stage contributes latency and can limit throughput. For example, slow chaincode execution lengthens endorsement time; a conservative BatchTimeout delays block creation; overloaded peers increase validation and commit delays. Network latency between components adds propagation time. Infrastructure bottlenecks such as C P U, insufficient memory, or low input and output throughput on peer hosts will show up as spikes in endorsement or commit times. A useful mental model is to trace a single transaction: client submits request, endorsing peers run chaincode and return a response, orderers batch transactions, peers validate and commit blocks. The slowest element on that path often dictates perceived latency. An actionable first step is to measure per-stage timings: how long endorsement takes, how frequently blocks are cut, and how long validation/commit takes. That data lets you focus tuning effort where it matters: faster chaincode, tuned batching, or added compute. As you proceed, remember a common misconception: improving one stage without measuring others can shift the bottleneck rather than remove it. Ask yourself after each change: what metric moved and what moved next?

Two parameters in the ordering service shape block creation: BatchSize and BatchTimeout. BatchSize sets the maximum number of transactions or block byte size before the orderer cuts a block. BatchTimeout is the maximum time the orderer will wait before cutting a block even if BatchSize isn’t reached. Larger BatchSize usually increases throughput because more transactions are grouped, reducing per-transaction overhead and improving network and storage efficiency. However, larger blocks increase propagation time and mean an individual transaction may wait longer before being committed, increasing latency. Smaller BatchTimeout reduces latency by cutting blocks more frequently, but when transaction arrival rate is low it can lead to many small blocks and lower throughput. Choosing values depends on your workload: a sustained high transaction rate favors larger BatchSize; low but latency-sensitive traffic favors small BatchTimeout. A practical approach is to iterate: measure current TPS and latency, try doubling BatchSize or halving BatchTimeout in a dev channel, and observe orderer logs and block finalization times. Remember to recreate or update channel configuration when you change channel-scoped parameters. A common misconception is that larger BatchSize is always better — it is better only when the network can process larger blocks without propagation or validation becoming new bottlenecks.

This walkthrough shows the minimal steps to change BatchTimeout in a development environment and observe the effect. Start by bringing up the test-network with defaults, then watch the orderer logs to see how often blocks are written. Next, edit configtx. yaml to change BatchTimeout from the default (often two seconds) to a new value such as five seconds or 500 milliseconds depending on your goal. Recreate the channel in the dev network so the new channel configuration takes effect. Finally, monitor the orderer logs for writeBlock messages to confirm block creation frequency changed as expected. This process is safe in a dev environment and is the quickest way to confirm tuning behavior before attempting a channel update in production. A common misconception is that changing the local orderer container setting will affect an existing channel immediately — channel-scoped batch parameters require channel config updates or channel recreation. Remember to capture metrics both before and after the change so you can quantify the impact on latency and throughput, and to test with realistic invoke scripts so BatchSize behaviors become visible when transaction rate varies.

Peers are responsible for endorsement, validation, and commitment. They run chaincode, maintain state databases, and write blocks to disk. Because of these roles, peer hosts need balanced C P U, memory, and disk input and output. Endorsement is C P U and memory heavy when chaincode executes complex logic; state writes and CouchDB queries can be input and output bound. A common operational error is under-provisioning disk input and output for peers running CouchDB, causing slow queries and backpressure. Monitoring is essential: track C P U and memory usage on peer hosts, disk input and output wait times, and network throughput. Instrument peer process metrics for endorsement durations, commit durations, and chaincode execution time. When you see endorsement time climb, profile chaincode to find inefficient loops or excessive ledger reads. When commit or validation slows, check disk input and output and peer process queue lengths. Scale horizontally by adding peers to share endorsement load or vertically by increasing C P U/memory where appropriate. Another common misconception is to scale only orderers when throughput suffers — often peers are the bottleneck. Always pair monitoring with targeted remediation: if CouchDB queries are slow, add indexes; if endorsement time is high, optimize chaincode or add endorsing peers.

Fabric peers support two state database options: LevelDB and CouchDB. LevelDB is the default embedded key-value store and is efficient for simple key lookups and range queries. CouchDB runs as a separate process, often in another container, and introduces network and serialization overhead. For query-heavy applications that need JSON document access and indexed searches, CouchDB is generally the correct choice — provided that you create appropriate indexes. Without indexes, CouchDB will perform full database scans for rich queries, causing severe performance degradation. A practical rule: prefer LevelDB when your workload is dominated by direct key lookups or range scans; prefer CouchDB when you need expressive JSON queries and can maintain appropriate indexes. Measure query latency under realistic load in both modes before committing to one in production. Remember that choosing CouchDB also means managing an additional process and ensuring indexes are deployed with your chaincode or database configuration.

CouchDB needs JSON index definitions so rich queries can run efficiently. An index declares the fields CouchDB should use to locate documents quickly. For example, if your application frequently queries by owner and status, you should create an index that includes those fields plus docType if you use it. Creating and deploying an index prevents full database scans. The example index is a small JSON document that names the index and lists fields. Deploy the index alongside chaincode or place it in the CouchDB design documents so the peer will use it for queries. Without this step, queries that filter by non-key attributes will degrade to full scans as the ledger grows. After deploying an index, re-run queries and measure latency — you should see a significant reduction. A common misconception is that CouchDB automatically indexes all fields; it does not. You must explicitly define indexes for the queries you plan to run frequently. Keep index definitions targeted to avoid unnecessary indexing overhead.
